PARTIAL — ITS "NOT ESTABLISHED" CLAUSE IS ANSWERED AND ITS CENTRAL CLAIM IS CONFIRMED, SO THE NODE STAYS OPEN. That fact closes with "NOT ESTABLISHED: how long a full `reflow2-core` rebuild actually takes, or what a crate split would save. The compile-unit argument is READ FROM RUST'S MODEL, NOT TIMED." It has now been timed, hours later, on the same day.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT DID TO IT: confirmed it, and bounded it. Its reasoning — that the crate is the compilation unit so a struct split cannot help — is right, and touching a one-impl-block leaf costs the same as touching the 54-method god-struct (13.74-14.09s workspace either way). What it could not say, and now can: the whole crate rebuilds in ~4s, so a CRATE split has a ceiling of about four seconds, which is not a restructure that pays for itself either. The fact argued the struct split was the wrong remedy; the measurement adds that the remedy it pointed at is barely worth taking.

⭐ AND IT SURFACED SOMETHING NEITHER NODE PREDICTED: ~10 of the 14 seconds is `reflow2-mcp` rebuilding behind core, so the dominant lever is the core→mcp dependency rather than anything inside core.

🛑 EVERYTHING ELSE IN THAT FACT IS UNTOUCHED and is the reason it stays open: its confirmation of global coupling and write contention, its finding that two of the three proposed remedies (ECS, opaque handles) collide with deliberate decisions, and its observation that the zero-crate-boundary seam result is arithmetic rather than a finding. Only the timing clause moved.
